slides.0.title: Winemaking and terroir in depth
slides.0.subtitle: Taming Tannat, botrytis, raisining and distillation
slides.1.title: Taming Tannat
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Micro-oxygenation
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Invented by Patrick Ducournau in Madiran in 1991 and authorised by the European Commission in 1996 (Wine With Seth); usually applied between alcoholic and malolactic fermentation (wein.plus)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Dosage and conditions
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Before malolactic fermentation up to 20–60 mg/L a month for two to six weeks; afterwards 0.5–2 mg/L a month; 15–20 °C recommended (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Risks
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Over-oxygenation gives dry harsh tannins and can raise volatile acidity and Brettanomyces; low-phenolic wines are unsuitable (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: MOX makes young Tannat approachable earlier, but it is not mandatory.
slides.2.title: Choices in Madiran
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Mandatory destemming
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Oak ageing
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Barrel ageing is common but not required; quality producers often age 12–24 months, and top cuvées spend 14–16 months in new French oak (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: The no-MOX route
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Producers such as Alain Brumont avoid MOX and rely on careful extraction and ripe fruit (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.content: Within one AOC there are two philosophies: taming and not taming.
slides.3.title: Two routes to sweetness
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Botrytis: Monbazillac
slides.3.highlights.0.content: All fruit must be botrytised and is hand-picked in successive tries; classic wines need at least 45 g/L and SGN at least 85 g/L (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Raisining: Jurançon
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Petit Manseng hangs on the vine until November or December, dried by the foehn; average yield is about 15 hL/ha, and top sweet cuvées go as low as 9 hL/ha (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Different mechanisms
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Jurançon's thick skins keep botrytis out, so concentration comes from desiccation rather than noble rot (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.content: Both are sweet, but Monbazillac comes from mould and Jurançon from wind.
slides.4.title: Sparkling and distillation
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Gaillac's ancestral method
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Méthode Gaillacoise uses only Mauzac with a single fermentation completed in the bottle and no added sugar (Wine With Seth); Mauzac ripens late, and traditional late picking kept residual sugar for a natural spring second fermentation (Wikipedia)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Armagnac
slides.4.highlights.1.content: A single continuous distillation leaving the still at 52–63%; aged in 400–420 L oak barrels and reduced to 40% before bottling; fermentation takes about 10–17 days to give a wine of 8–9.5% (wein.plus)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Terroir influence
slides.4.highlights.2.content: Bas-Armagnac's poor acidic clay-loam gives light fruity spirits, while Ténarèze's heavy clay-limestone gives fuller spirits that peak after long ageing (armagnac.fr)
slides.4.content: With sparkling, sweet and spirits in one region, it is a crossroads of techniques.
